newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Euro tobacco stocks hit by cancer link.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Euro tobacco stocks hit by cancer link.

text.p: European tobacco shares fell on Monday amid fears that new evidence to suggest a direct link between smoking and lung cancer could strengthen litigation against the tobacco giants.
Scientists in the United States said they had identified a substance in the tar of tobacco smoke that directly transforms human lung tissue.
The findings, published in the prestigious Science journal on Friday, are the first direct link to be found between smoking and cancer.
The Tobacco Advisory Council said today it had no comment to make on the study.

Shares in Britain's BAT Industries, and Imperial Tobacco reacted negatively on speculation that lawsuits, already rife in the United States, would increase if the study can lead to proof of causation.
In France, shares in tobacco group Seita, makers of the Gitanes and Gauloises brands of cigarettes lost almost four percent.
In Spain, meanwhile, shares in the majority state-owned Tabacalera fell two percent on the latest findings.

Britain's BAT Industries which is already heavily exposed to U.S. litigation through its Brown & Williamson unit, makers of Kent, Kool and State Express cigarettes, closed down seven pence at 424p after hitting a low of 420p. The shares have fallen dramatically since January when they were valued at 580p.

Brown & Williamson said in a statement today that the U.S. study did not compare its results in smokers with those in non-smokers and it was therefore impossible to tell whether the changes identified were related to smoking.
"The authors of the study limit their conclusions severely by saying that their results are only "suggestive," the statement said.
Nevertheless, analysts said tobacco shares would still be in for a bumpy ride as investors digest the latest in a long-line of negative comment.
Imperial Tobacco, recently spun-off from the demerged Hanson group has a 38 percent share of the British tobacco market.

Analysts said its share price has been shielded to some degree by the group's lack of U.S. sales. On Monday the shares managed to recoup an earlier loss to close four pence higher at 383p, rebounding from a low of 376p.

"The problem with tobacco stocks is that there is a platoon of American lawyers chipping away at your share price and they'll just keep on going and going," said one head of equity sales at a leading brokerage in London.
But though short-term reaction was to be expected some analysts said the downside had been overdone.

"The point is that the link has only just been proved, and was not known at the time before warnings were in place, so it does not necessarily strengthen the plaintiffs' case that much," said Nyren Scott-Malden, analyst at BZW, commenting on current litigation against the tobacco manufacturers.
Ironically, in the long-term some analysts believe that tobacco sales could benefit if the element in smoke that causes cancer can be found.
"The industry can then try to reduce that element to make cigarettes safer, which could actually help sales in the longer term," Nyren Scott-Malden added.
